notes:
I've written notes for most verses of Hebrews 10, mostly from older commentaries and a few modern evangelical teachers. There are real gaps. I found nothing from Lutheran, Orthodox or Pentecostal-denomination sources (ag.org, pneumareview), nothing from modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org), and nothing on hyper-grace or prosperity readings, so those are left out. I also didn't fetch the Pulpit Commentary, and the full Gill, Ellicott and Enduring Word pages came back incomplete, so vv. 21 and 32–33 are thin. Ellicott's notes on vv. 10–39 come from search snippets rather than the full page. Barnes, Benson, Gill and others are quoted unnamed on BibleHub's combined verse pages, so I've written "a commentator" for those. Enduring Word (David Guzik) is listed under your Pentecostal heading, but nothing in what I read speaks for a Pentecostal tradition, so I've treated him as a general evangelical voice.

## Hebrews 10 – Research Notes

**v. 1**
- The "shadow" isn't bad, just incomplete. The Old Covenant law wasn't evil, but it couldn't fully cleanse from sin or save. Guzik also cites Newell: a shadow can't show features accurately the way a true image (*eikon*) does. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- Ellicott notes that the Greek text in the second half of the verse is uncertain. The better manuscripts read "they [the priests] can never…". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/10.htm
- Gill (unnamed on the BibleHub page) says "the law" here means the ceremonial law, not the moral law, which is a plain rule of conduct rather than a shadow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/10-1.htm
- *Methodist:* Wesley says the law couldn't make anyone perfect in justification or in sanctification. He uses this to argue that Christian holiness should rise higher than what was attained under the old dispensation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**v. 2**
- Having to repeat sacrifices shows they were weak. If they had solved sin, they would have stopped. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- A commentator on BibleHub compares the sacrifices to medicine that has to be taken again and again because it never cures. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/10-2.htm
- *Methodist:* For Wesley, someone fully cleansed would no longer be conscious of either the guilt or the power of their sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm
- *Brethren:* Kelly says "conscience of sins" doesn't mean believers never sin or never notice failure. It means dread that God will judge them for their sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/10-26.html

**v. 3**
- In each of his three prayers on the Day of Atonement, the high priest openly confessed sin (Ellicott). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/10.htm
- Wesley: the yearly public remembrance of sins proves their guilt hadn't been fully removed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**v. 4**
- Animal sacrifice could cover sin (Guzik says the Hebrew word for atonement means "to cover") but could never take it away. Morris adds that the Greek word for "take away" means complete removal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- Ellicott: the sacrifices did their job, but they couldn't remove the need for a better offering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/10.htm

**vv. 5–7**
- The quotation is Psalm 40 in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), which reads "body" where the Hebrew reads "ears". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- Ellicott: the Hebrew ("ears you have dug for me") means God gave the psalmist the ability to hear and obey. He thinks the Greek translators were paraphrasing that meaning, and that the author's argument doesn't depend on the word "body". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/10.htm
- Ellicott: David's words were only partly true of himself and are fulfilled in the Son of David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/10.htm
- Barclay: both readings mean the same thing, a life given to obeying God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/hebrews-10.html
- Bruce (via Guzik): Jesus' becoming human was itself an act of submission, pointing ahead to His death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- Wesley: the text says "into the world", not "into the tabernacle", because the whole world has a stake in His sacrifice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**vv. 8–9**
- Ellicott: the shift from "the law" to "law" may contrast any outward ritual law with inward obedience. The "first" (animal sacrifices) is removed to establish the "second" (doing God's will). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/10.htm
- Wesley: Christ sets aside the legal arrangement to establish the gospel one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: better translated "in which will we have been sanctified". Because the offering was made once for all, the sanctifying was also done once for all. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hebrews-10.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: this is Christ's finished work setting believers apart permanently, not the gradual process of growing in holiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/hebrews-10.html
- Wesley: "sanctified" means cleansed from guilt and dedicated to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm
- **Catholic vs. Protestant (the Mass), covering vv. 10–18:**
  - *Catholic.com:* the Mass isn't a separate sacrifice. Quoting the Council of Trent, it is the one sacrifice of the Cross made present again, offered in an "unbloody manner". https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/once-for-all
  - *Catholic.com:* the Church says Christ's work is made present at the Mass, not repeated, and His death happened once for all. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/is-the-mass-a-true-sacrifice
  - *Baptist (MacArthur):* the Lord's Supper is only a remembrance, and the idea of re-sacrificing Christ in the Mass is blasphemous. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/80-123/The-Sufficiency-of-Christs-Sacrifice
  - *GotQuestions:* the Catholic teaching contradicts "once for all" (Heb 10:10; 1 Pet 3:18). https://www.gotquestions.org/transubstantiation.html
  - Guzik quotes Robertson asking how priests who call the Mass a repetition of Christ's sacrifice can explain this verse. He also cites Bruce, who blames a weak Latin Vulgate translation for the Western idea of a repeated offering. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/

**vv. 11–12**
- The priests always stood because their work was never done. Jesus sat down because His was finished, though He still intercedes for His people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- Gill (unnamed on BibleHub): the present tense is used because the sacrifices were still going on when the letter was written. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/10-11.htm
- Ellicott: "sat down" (Psalm 110:1) adds a king's dignity to the priestly picture. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/10.htm
- Wesley: the priest stands like a servant; Christ sits like a son, in honour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**v. 13**
- This looks ahead to Christ's return and His final triumph over every enemy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- JFB: the enemies are Satan and Death, whose strength is sin. Once sin is taken away, their defeat must follow. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/hebrews-10.html

**v. 14**
- Guzik: Christ's work could save anyone but actually saves only "those who are being sanctified". Spurgeon: they are made perfectly free from guilt, not perfect in character. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- BibleHub study notes: this is both a finished standing and an ongoing transformation. https://biblehub.com/hebrews/10-14.htm
- Wesley: "perfected" means everything needed for full reconciliation with God has been done. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm
- *Catholic:* Karlo Broussard answers James White's argument that the Mass can't be Christ's sacrifice because people don't leave it "perfected". He says "being sanctified" already implies an incomplete state, and the gap lies in our disposition, not in Christ's sacrifice. https://www.catholic.com/audio/drk/is-the-mass-the-same-sacrifice-as-calvary-a-response-to-james-white

**vv. 15–17**
- The passage presents the Holy Spirit as the LORD speaking. Thomas sees the Trinity here: the Father's will (v. 9), Christ's work (v. 12), the Spirit's witness (v. 15). The new covenant promises inner change and complete forgiveness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- Wesley: the new covenant is now fully ratified, so any repetition of Christ's offering is "utterly needless". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**v. 18**
- Guzik, citing Newell: this ends the teaching section of the letter, and exhortation follows. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- *Catholic:* the Mass isn't a new offering for sin but a fresh sharing in the one sacrifice of Calvary. https://www.catholic.com/qa/why-the-mass-when-theres-no-need-for-sin-offering

**vv. 19–20**
- Ellicott: this resembles the appeal in 4:14–16. Believers don't enter "with blood" the way the high priest did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/10-19.htm
- "New and living": a living Jesus brings us into God's presence. The torn veil matches His torn body. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- Wesley: when Christ's body was wounded, God was revealed and the way to heaven opened. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**v. 22**
- The command would only be needed if they were struggling to draw near; Guzik sees this lost closeness as their real problem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- Wesley reads "bodies washed" as a blameless, holy way of life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**v. 23**
- Discouragement had made them waver; renewed confidence in Jesus would steady them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- Wesley: the "hope we profess" is the hope professed at baptism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**vv. 24–25**
- JFB: "consider" means paying close attention to fellow believers' needs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/hebrews-10.html
- Wesley: some stayed away out of fear of persecution, or thinking they were "above external ordinances". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm
- Matthew Henry: some were already leaving the meetings and starting to drift away from the faith itself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/10-29.html
- Bengel (on BibleHub): lukewarm attendance can lead to apostasy, which links v. 25 to v. 26. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/10-26.htm

**vv. 26–27: the main Protestant disagreement**
- *Shared reading:* this is falling away from the faith (apostasy), not ordinary sin. Bengel: "to sin" here means total revolt from God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/10-26.htm
- Ellicott: they had "full knowledge" of the truth, and the offering they reject has abolished all the earlier sacrifices. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hebrews-10.html
- **Calvinist / Reformed Baptist:** MacArthur calls this perhaps the most serious warning in Scripture, and says the apostate shows he was never born again. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1026-27
- **Methodist / Arminian:** Wesley says "we" means any Christian, and the sin is "total apostasy from God", called "drawing back" in v. 38. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm
- **Church of Christ (Coffman):** the claim that apostasy is impossible ("final perseverance") isn't New Testament teaching and can lead to presumption. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/10-26.html
- **Guzik (middle position):** the debate is partly about words, but the warnings aren't hypothetical. People who appear to be believers can be lost. https://enduringword.com/can-you-lose-your-salvation-hebrews-1026/
- He stresses that even people who believe salvation can't be lost should take these warnings seriously. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/how-do-you-interpret-hebrews-1026-27/
- **Free Grace view (bible.org):** this is about real believers. The danger is God's judgment in this life and loss of rewards. The NIV's "keep on sinning" overstates the Greek tense. https://bible.org/question/hebrews-1026-30-speaking-believers-or-unbelievers
- **Catholic:** Karlo Broussard calls vv. 26–27 a "death blow" to the idea that future sins are already forgiven. https://www.catholic.com/audio/are-your-future-sins-forgiven

**v. 28**
- The Mosaic death penalty for covenant violation (Deut 17:2–7). https://biblehub.com/q/Hebrews_10_29_on_apostasy_consequences.htm
- Wesley limits it to capital cases of presumptuous law-breaking. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**v. 29: who was "sanctified"?**
- **Owen (Reformed):** it refers to Christ, who was set apart as high priest, not to the apostate. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1026-27
- GotQuestions sets out three readings: believers who lose salvation, believers who keep it but face discipline, or false converts (with Christ as the one sanctified). https://www.gotquestions.org/sanctified-Hebrews.html
- Another Reformed answer (a note on BibleHub): it means outward dedication through baptism and profession, not inward holiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/10-29.htm
- **Piper (Baptist):** the "sanctified" of v. 29 isn't the same as in v. 14. These were hypocrites who still received grace bought by Christ's blood. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/woe-to-those-who-trample-the-son-of-god
- **Wesley:** Christ died for him too, and "he was at least justified once." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm
- **Dispensational (Constable):** the apostate is a Christian. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/10-29.html

**vv. 30–31**
- Wesley: God will judge His own people more strictly than the heathen if they rebel. To "fall into the hands" means to fall into His avenging justice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**vv. 32–34**
- Guzik, quoting Trapp: "publicly exposed" literally means set on a theatre stage. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-10/
- Ellicott: the Greek word for "conflict" comes from athletic contests. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/10.htm
- Ellicott: once the correct text of v. 34 is restored, it says nothing about who wrote the letter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hebrews.html
- Wesley (following the KJV "me in my bonds"): they sympathised with all suffering believers, especially the writer, and gladly lost their goods. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**vv. 35–36**
- Ellicott: throwing away confidence is the opposite of holding it fast (3:6). "Patience" means brave endurance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/10.htm
- Guzik: the picture is a soldier throwing away his shield. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/por/tew/hebrews-10.html (Portuguese translation of his commentary)
- Wesley: no one can take your confidence from you except yourself. "The promise" means perfect love and eternal life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): confidence is freedom to approach God, and you can lose it if you aren't faithful. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/10-35.html
- GotQuestions: v. 36 sums up the message of the whole letter. https://www.gotquestions.org/you-have-need-of-endurance.html

**vv. 37–38**
- Ellicott: the writer follows the Greek Old Testament of Habakkuk, reversing the order of the clauses. The Hebrew word usually translated "faith" almost always means faithfulness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/10.htm
- Wesley: the righteous live by faith "as long as he retains that gift". Drawing back means wrecking your faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm

**v. 39**
- A confident conclusion: "we" are those who persevere. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/por/tew/hebrews-10.html
- Ellicott links it to Jesus' sayings about losing or gaining one's soul (Luke 9:25; 21:19). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/10.htm
- Wesley: "those who have faith" means those who believe to the end. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/10.htm
